missions.name: OPS-SAT
missions.identity: ESA operations technology demonstrator. This is OPS-SAT, not the separately proposed OPS-SAT2.
missions.description: Operate a flying laboratory to test new mission control techniques and onboard satellite software. Upload experiment software to a reconfigurable processing platform, run the experiments under a protective spacecraft bus and downlink experiment results.
missions.epoch: 18 December 2019 injection orbit, mission ended in May 2024
missions.statusDetail: Historical injection conditions from ESA. The mission completion notice reports the night of 22 to 23 May 2024. Not a current orbit.

altitudeKm.original: circular, polar orbit at 515 km altitude
altitudeKm.meaning: Reported flight injection altitude on 18 December 2019. Only this scalar altitude can be accepted as a new circular study assumption.

orbitType.meaning: Explicit ESA orbit classification for the injection. No numerical inclination is inferred from the word polar.

sources.title: ESA, OPS-SAT mission overview
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
sources.location: Opening mission-completion notice, mission description and Project status section
quotes: A flying laboratory, ESA's OPS-SAT is the first of its kind, with the sole purpose of testing and validating new techniques in mission control and on-board satellite systems.
Launch took place on 18 December, 2019, when OPS-SAT was injected into a circular, polar orbit at 515 km altitude.
The S-band link will be used to upload experimenter’s’ software and download results of on-board experiments.

caveats: The 500 to 600 km orbit in a separate OPS-SAT2 concept is not used for OPS-SAT.
OPS-SAT software experiment safety architecture is mission context. No EPS architecture or load profile is copied.

missions.name: Proba-V
missions.identity: ESA PROBA-V vegetation monitoring minisatellite, launched on 7 May 2013. It is not a CubeSat.
missions.description: Map land cover and vegetation growth across the planet with an Earth imaging instrument. Collect blue, red, near-infrared and mid-infrared observations for crop monitoring, vegetation classification, plant and forest growth, and inland water studies.
missions.epoch: ESA mission parameters for the mission launched in 2013, operational phase ended 30 June 2020
missions.statusDetail: Experimental operations continued from 1 July 2020 to 31 October 2021. The table gives mission orbit context, not current orbital elements.

altitudeKm.meaning: Orbit Altitude in the ESA Mission Parameters table. A nominal mission parameter, not a current measured altitude or a guaranteed launch option.

orbitType.meaning: Orbit Type in the ESA mission table. This context does not enable SSO dynamics in the EPS engine.

inclinationDeg.meaning: Orbit Inclination in the ESA mission table. Context only.

sources.title: ESA Earth Online, PROBA-V mission overview
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
sources.location: About PROBA-V, Mission Parameters table and PROBA-V Objectives
quotes: PROBA-V, launched on 7 May 2013, is a miniaturised ESA satellite tasked with a full-scale mission to map land cover and vegetation growth across the entire planet every two days.
Polar Earth Sun-synchronous
98.73 degrees
820 km

The PROBA-V imager's continent-spanning 2250 km field of view collects light in the blue, red, near-infrared and mid-infrared wavebands, ideal for monitoring plant and forest growth as well as inland water bodies.

caveats: Proba-V is a minisatellite analogue for operations, not a CubeSat hardware or EPS template.
The source reports degraded illumination at the end of the operational phase. The demo models no seasonal or local-time evolution.

missions.name: RainCube
missions.identity: NASA/JPL Radar in a CubeSat technology demonstrator. The flown single satellite is distinct from a proposed future constellation.
missions.description: Demonstrate a compact Ka-band precipitation radar on a small satellite. Transmit radar signals toward storms and measure echoes from rain and snow to reveal the vertical structure of precipitation inside clouds. Return storm observations as a technology demonstration.
missions.epoch: Flown mission, deorbited 24 December 2020 as reported by NASA ESTO on 22 June 2021
missions.statusDetail: JPL reports successful storm measurements after deployment from the ISS. No numerical spacecraft altitude is supplied by the reviewed JPL article.

orbitType.meaning: Explicit deployment orbit class in the JPL report. ISS deployment alone is not used to invent altitude or inclination.

sources.title: NASA/JPL, NASA Tests Tiny Satellites to Track Global Storms
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
sources.location: Mission description and Seeing the Bigger Picture section
quotes: RainCube is a technology-demonstration mission to enable Ka-band precipitation radar technologies on a low-cost, quick-turnaround platform.
RainCube was deployed into low-Earth orbit from the International Space Station in July.
The satellite's umbrella-like antenna sends out chirps, or specialized radar signals, that bounce off raindrops, bringing back a picture of what the inside of the storm looks like.

sources.title: NASA ESTO, TEMPEST-D deorbits after successfully validating advanced remote-sensing instruments
sources.location: 22 June 2021 mission completion report, opening and deployment/deorbit paragraphs
quotes: RainCube deorbited on December 24, 2020.

A team of astronauts then deployed TEMPEST-D from ISS into Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where it validated the new-to-space instrumentation and a passive drag technique to position a number of small satellites into a working constellation.

Specifically, they deployed instruments on board a small satellite to capture novel datasets for studying Earth’s atmosphere as a storm evolves and innovate new approaches for sampling atmospheric temperature and humidity across multiple frequency bands.

caveats: The future fleet described in the article is a concept, not the flown single RainCube mission.
No altitude or inclination is inferred from the ISS deployment or from the storm target height.

missions.name: ASTERIA
missions.identity: Arcsecond Space Telescope Enabling Research in Astrophysics, a NASA/JPL and MIT CubeSat technology demonstration.
missions.description: Observe nearby stars with a compact space telescope and measure their brightness precisely. Demonstrate stellar photometry technologies for detecting exoplanet transits through dips in starlight, with extended experiments in autonomous CubeSat operations.
missions.epoch: Orbit described in June 2019 report (overview as of September 2018), status update 3 January 2020
missions.statusDetail: Historical approximate flight orbit with no measurement epoch specified. The later JPL status article reports loss of contact. These are not current orbital elements.

altitudeKm.meaning: Approximate historical altitude explicitly stated in the mission orbit description, Section 1.3. The report is dated June 2019 and its overview covers September 2018. No orbit measurement epoch is supplied.

orbitType.original: ASTERIA deployed into low-Earth orbit in November 2017
orbitType.meaning: Orbit class explicitly stated in the mission overview. No circularity is inferred from ISS deployment.

inclinationDeg.meaning: Historical inclination explicitly stated in Section 1.3, not inferred from the ISS. Context only.

sources.title: NASA/JPL, Tiny Satellite for Studying Distant Planets Goes Quiet
sources.location: Opening status paragraphs and stellar photometry description
quotes: Deployed into Earth orbit from the space station on Nov. 20, 2017, the technology demonstration mission showed that many technologies necessary for studying and potentially finding exoplanets (planets orbiting stars other than our Sun) can be shrunk to fit on small satellites.
ASTERIA observed a handful of nearby stars and successfully demonstrated that it could achieve precision measurements of the stars' brightness.
The last successful communication with ASTERIA, short for Arcsecond Space Telescope Enabling Research in Astrophysics, was on Dec. 5; attempts to contact it are expected to continue into March 2020.

sources.title: Babuscia et al., Arcsecond Space Telescope Enabling Research in Astrophysics (ASTERIA) Telecommunications
sources.revision: NASA/JPL Near Earth Design and Performance Summary Series, Article 2, June 2019
sources.location: Section 1, printed p. 1 (overview), Section 1.3, printed p. 4 / PDF p. 18 (orbit)
quotes: ASTERIA deployed into low-Earth orbit in November 2017
approximately 400 km altitude, 51.6° inclination.
the eclipse duration varies as a function of the beta angle

caveats: The orbit values are explicitly reported in Section 1.3. They are not inferred from deployment from the space station or taken only from a link-budget simulation.
The report describes beta-angle-dependent eclipse variation. The EPS demo uses simplified circular geometry and does not reproduce that variation.
This record makes no exoplanet discovery claim.

missions.name: AAUSAT4
missions.identity: Aalborg University student CubeSat in the ESA Fly Your Satellite! programme. Distinct from AAUSAT5.
missions.description: Test an Automatic Identification System receiver in orbit to identify and track ships carrying AIS transponders in remote waters and away from coastal areas. Receive maritime tracking signals to support monitoring of shipping lanes.
missions.epoch: Initial deployment report following the 25 April 2016 launch
missions.statusDetail: Approximate initial flight orbit, reported before final orbital parameters were confirmed. These are not current orbital elements.

altitudeKm.original: swinging from about 665 km to 453 km and back again
altitudeKm.meaning: Approximate initial flight altitude range in the deployment report. Final values were still to be confirmed. No scalar circular altitude is available to apply.

orbitType.meaning: Explicit orbit classification in the deployment report. Elliptical geometry is outside this EPS demo.

sources.title: ESA, Student satellites fly freely on their orbit in space
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
sources.location: CubeSat deployment orbit paragraph and final mission summaries
quotes: The CubeSats are positioned in an elliptical Low Earth Orbit (LEO), swinging from about 665 km to 453 km and back again.
The final orbital parameters will be confirmed in the next few hours.
AAUSAT4, University of Aalborg, Denmark, will operate an Automated Identification System (AIS) receiver in order to identify and track the position of ships transiting away from coastal areas.

sources.title: ESA, Student teams to launch
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
quotes: 25 April 2016

AAUSAT4 will conduct in-orbit testing of an improved version of the Automated Identification System (AIS) receiver, a system developed by the Aalborg students to track and identify ships and other vehicles carrying an AIS transponder, which are transiting away from coastal areas and in remote areas, to enable safer use of new shipping lanes.

caveats: The separate prelaunch table reports approximately 454 by 682 km and 98.2 degrees. Those intended parameters are not merged into the initial flight orbit.
AAUSAT4 and the ISS-deployed AAUSAT5 are different spacecraft.

missions.name: TEMPEST-D
missions.identity: Temporal Experiment for Storms and Tropical Systems Demonstration, led by Colorado State University with NASA/JPL and partners.
missions.description: Demonstrate miniature microwave radiometer sensors for observing Earth weather. Measure atmospheric temperature and humidity across multiple frequency bands as tropical storms evolve, and return observations of hurricane moisture and rainfall structure.
missions.epoch: 28 August 2019 hurricane observation, mission completion reported 22 June 2021
missions.statusDetail: Flown CubeSat deployed in 2018. NASA ESTO reports that the mission ended after nearly three years as the spacecraft deorbited.

orbitType.meaning: Explicit deployment orbit class in the NASA ESTO completion report.

sources.title: NASA ESTO, TEMPEST-D deorbits after successfully validating advanced remote-sensing instruments
sources.location: 22 June 2021 mission completion report, opening and deployment/deorbit paragraphs
quotes: RainCube deorbited on December 24, 2020.

A team of astronauts then deployed TEMPEST-D from ISS into Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where it validated the new-to-space instrumentation and a passive drag technique to position a number of small satellites into a working constellation.

Specifically, they deployed instruments on board a small satellite to capture novel datasets for studying Earth’s atmosphere as a storm evolves and innovate new approaches for sampling atmospheric temperature and humidity across multiple frequency bands.

sources.title: NASA/JPL, Small Satellite TEMPEST-D Sees Hurricane Dorian off Coast
sources.revision: No explicit page revision stated. Reviewed retrieved content.
sources.location: Image PIA23414 caption, observation on 28 August 2019
quotes: At a vantage point 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the storm, the CubeSat used its miniaturized radio-wave-based instrument to see through the clouds, revealing areas with strong rain and moisture being pulled into the storm.
The radiometer instrument was built by JPL and employs high-frequency microwave amplifier technology developed by Northrop Grumman.

caveats: The image caption quotes approximately 400 km above a storm, not precision Earth-referenced orbital elements. A transferable scalar altitude is left missing in this record.
TEMPEST-D used a microwave radiometer. It is distinct from the active precipitation radar carried by RainCube.

missions.name: RAX-2
missions.identity: Radio Aurora Explorer 2, University of Michigan and SRI International. This record is specific to RAX-2.
missions.description: Study magnetic field-aligned plasma irregularities in the lower polar ionosphere. Receive scattered ground radar signals with an onboard receiver during experiments, save measurements with position and time information, then process, compress and downlink the science data.
missions.epoch: Reported in 2012 after the 28 October 2011 launch
missions.statusDetail: Historical mission report. These are not current orbital elements.

altitudeKm.original: The RAX-2 spacecraft is in a 410 by 820 kilometer, 101.5 degree inclination orbit.
altitudeKm.meaning: Reported flight altitude pair, retained as a 410 to 820 km interval. It is not a scalar circular altitude. No midpoint will be applied.

inclinationDeg.meaning: Inclination explicitly reported for RAX-2 in the 2012 article. Context only.

sources.title: Spangelo et al. (2012), Applying Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to a Standard CubeSat
sources.location: Section 5, pp. 3-4 (ConOps and orbit), Section 11, p. 8 (launch)
quotes: RAX-2 is the reference CubeSat Mission the SysML team has chosen as the basis for building the CubeSat Modeling Framework.
The RAX-2 spacecraft is in a 410 by 820 kilometer, 101.5 degree inclination orbit.
During a typical science experiment, scattered signals are detected by the on-board radar receiver (payload) and are saved to the spacecraft flash memory.
Data are then processed, compressed, and transmitted to the ground.
For RAX-2, the Launch Service consisted of the launch on a Delta II rocket from the Vandenberg Air Force Base in California on October 28, 2011.

caveats: The 80 to 300 km ionosphere target region is not the spacecraft altitude.
The 2014 MBSE simulation trade-study altitudes are excluded. That paper explicitly says its model is not intended to be an accurate model of the RAX satellite.
This source gives an altitude pair rather than the scalar circular input required by the EPS demo. Orbit type is left missing because no explicit classification was retained in this source record.

missions.name: UM5-SAT (EPS case study)
missions.identity: The UM5-SAT case study in El Hachimi et al. (2025). This record is not assigned to the separately named UM5-Ribat or UM5-EOSAT spacecraft.
missions.description: Collect short messages from Internet of Things terminals across Morocco with a software defined radio payload and relay the data to the ground station in Rabat during visibility windows. Alternate receiving, ground communication, idle and safe modes to support agriculture, environmental monitoring and disaster management.
missions.epoch: 2025 publication, with a July 2024 simulation scenario
missions.statusDetail: Specified case-study orbit. It is not presented here as a measured flight orbit or a claim about launch status.

orbitType.original: A Sun-Synchronous Orbit at 550 km altitude
orbitType.meaning: Intended orbit classification in Section 6.1. The EPS demo does not propagate Sun-synchronous dynamics.

inclinationDeg.meaning: Specified study inclination in Table 6. Table 6 supplies a clear degree unit despite an inconsistent unit in the extracted Section 6.1 prose.

sources.title: El Hachimi et al. (2025), A Framework for sizing, designing, and testing of Electrical Power System for nanosatellites

Receiving Mode: The satellite is receiving short messages from IoT terminals on the ground.
A Sun-Synchronous Orbit at 550 km altitude

550km
